html:
In Mughal India, money changers and bankers called sarafs moved money and credit across the subcontinent with paper notes called hundis. A hundi worked much like a European bill of exchange.

A merchant in Surat could pay cash to a saraf there and get a hundi. His agent in Agra or Bengal took it to the saraf's partner, who paid out. No coin had to travel on dangerous roads. Hundis could also be dated ahead, which made them loans, and they could be sold on.

The sarafs also tested and changed the many coins in use, held deposits and lent to merchants, nobles and the state. Great banking houses grew from this trade. In Bengal, Jagat Seth was banker to the nawab; in Surat, Virji Vora lent to the English.

The European companies relied on these bankers. The East India Company borrowed from them and paid its bills through them. The system ran on trust between families and castes, often Marwari, Gujarati or Khatri. It still lives on in informal transfers, close kin of hawala.
